content: Egg white, also known as albumen or glaire, is the clear liquid found inside an egg. It constitutes the cytoplasm of the egg, which remains a single cell (including the yolk) until fertilization occurs. Egg white is primarily composed of approximately 15% proteins dissolved in water. Its main biological function is to protect the yolk and provide additional nutrition for the developing embryo, as it is rich in proteins and has high nutritional value. Unlike the yolk, egg white contains negligible fat. Egg whites are widely used in both culinary and non-culinary applications. They make up about two-thirds of the total weight of an egg (excluding the shell), with 90% of that weight being water. The remaining portion consists of proteins, trace minerals, small amounts of fatty material, vitamins, and glucose. A large egg white contains about 20 calories, 3 grams of carbohydrates, and 62 milligrams of sodium. Egg white is also free of dietary cholesterol, making it a popular choice for those aiming to reduce cholesterol intake in their diet. It contains approximately 40 different proteins, each with specific natural functions. Uses of Egg White: Egg whites are often separated and used in cooking for dishes such as meringues, soufflés, and some types of omelets. When beaten or cooked, egg white turns white, which is the origin of its name. In recipes requiring egg yolks, two egg whites can often substitute for one yolk. In educational settings, egg whites are used to teach students how to test for protein using Biuret reagent. Egg whites are used to clarify broths and remove sediments from champagne and beer. Historically, egg whites were used in the emulsion of traditional photographic paper. In medieval medicine, egg whites were applied to treat wounds and broken bones. Athletes and bodybuilders often consume egg whites as a lean protein source and health food supplement. Egg whites can also serve as a base for waterproof glues. Nutritional Considerations: Excessive consumption of raw egg whites over an extended period (months to years) can lead to biotin deficiency. This is due to the high levels of avidin, a protein in egg whites that binds strongly to the vitamin biotin, preventing its absorption. Denaturation of Egg White Proteins: Proteins in egg whites are composed of long chains of amino acids, which are tightly folded into a compact structure in their raw state. These structures are held together by chemical bonds and interactions between amino acids. When an egg is cooked, heat breaks these bonds in a process called denaturation. As the protein chains unfold and interact with neighboring proteins, new bonds form, resulting in a change in texture. Egg White Foam: Beating egg whites introduces physical stress, which can create a foam. This process involves two types of stress: 1. The whisk drags the liquid through itself, unfolding the protein molecules (denaturation). 2. Air is mixed into the whites, causing the proteins to come out of their natural state. The denatured proteins gather at the interface of air and water, forming bonds with other proteins and stabilizing the foam by trapping air. Stabilizing Egg White Foam: 1. Copper Bowls: Copper bowls have been used since the 18th century in France to stabilize egg foams. Copper reacts with sulfur-containing components in egg whites, forming tight bonds that prevent the sulfur from reacting with other materials. Silver-plated bowls or powdered copper supplements can achieve similar results. However, copper bowls are expensive and difficult to clean. Copper contamination from the bowl is minimal, with a cup of foam containing only a fraction of the daily recommended copper intake. 2. Adding Acid: Cream of tartar (potassium bitartrate) is an acidic salt that can lower the pH of egg whites by increasing the concentration of free hydrogen ions. This stabilizes the foam and serves as an alternative to using a copper bowl. The recommended amount is 0.5 grams of cream of tartar per egg white. Alternatively, 1/2 teaspoon (2 mL) of lemon juice can achieve the same effect.
